items.title: Delfeayo Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: When I did my first record with my dad, Syndrome, I think we used – maybe we used a little pickup.

ctx.x: Oh, you’re talking about back in New Orleans.

Ron Carter. No, he did his first CD with Ron Carter, and then I think Clarence Seay was on a song. At some point Ray Drummond played on the second recording. And Phil Bowler. He had a number of bassists. There was the concern of the lack of an acoustic sound, but also that that bass – it was something. The bass sounded – it was an electric signal, so that they could make it sound present, very present, but it didn’t fit the sound spectrum of the rest of the band. It’s like you had the rest of the band, and then…

When we did Trio Jeepy, which was with Milt Hinton, which was again – it was my idea, that I would like to get the younger and the older musicians involved. I kept telling – when Branford was on the road with Sting, he would call me. “Man, this is like constant recess. I’m dying out here. It’s like, ugh.” So I sent him some Ben Webster recordings. I started hanging out with Milt Hinton. I said, “Check out this guy, Ben Webster, ” which I’m sure he’d heard of Ben, but he didn’t really know him. He was like, “Man!”…

items.title: Ellis Marsalis interviewed by Monk Rowe, New Orleans, Louisiana, January 7, 2020
items.q: He has recorded as a leader and with his sons, Wynton, Branford, Delfeayo and Jason.

ctx.x: Pianist and educator Ellis Marsalis was born in New Orleans in 1934. He has performed and recorded with a diverse list of artists, including Al Hirt, Cannonball Adderley and Kermit Ruffins. Ellis taught extensively at the New Orleans Center for Creative Arts and helped launch the careers of Harry Connick Jr., Terrance Blanchard and Nicholas Payton. He has recorded as a leader and with his sons, Wynton, Branford, Delfeayo and Jason.
Ellis was interviewed in New Orleans, Louisiana on January 7, 2020 by Monk Rowe, Director of the Fillius Jazz Archive.

items.title: Ellis Marsalis — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I understand, from having talked to Jason and talked to Delfeayo before, and Wynton, that they have a great respect for their mother.

ctx.x: I cannot complete this interview without acknowledging and thanking with sincere gratitude Dolores, your wife. We had a chance to talk with her, because – when we first arrived, we had a chance to sit with her. Obviously there’s a woman of staunch,

staunch fortitude. I think about a career of a musician and the largeness of this family, having to move, and when you’re gone doing gigs and touring, she’s got these five, six, or how many ever are at home at that time. She just seems to have been an immeasurable contributor to the success of this family as well. And I understand, from having talked to Jason and talked to Delfeayo before, and Wynton, that they have a great respect for their mother. They have a tremendous love for their mother. I think that that…

She doesn’t even want to do any kind of biography or nothing, and it wouldn’t really be that difficult for her, because a young lady who is – because she got all of these young women who are like daughters that she never had. One of them, she was talking to her the other night. She lives in Washington. She works in the Obama administration, not for him directly, but she’s in the ethics area. She can write. If she really wanted to do it, there’s a lot of help out here. So I don’t know. She may decide to do it, and…
